question: to the Commission Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR), Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR), Georgiana Teodorescu (ECR), Geadis Geadi (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Ciaran Mullooly (Renew), Waldemar Tomaszewski (ECR), Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Katarína Roth Neveďalová (NI), Nikola Bartůšek (NI), Milan Zver (PPE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Flavio Tosi (PPE), Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI), Jessika van Leeuwen (ECR) Subject:

Food security in the European Union is under increasing pressure. Following the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, EU farmers are facing new external disruptions affecting production capacity and significantly increasing costs. This situation builds on the impact of the war in Ukraine, which drove up fertiliser prices. The introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) in 2026 led to a further price increase of 20-25 %, with urea rising from below EUR 500 per tonne to EUR 570-600 per tonne. In the context of the escalation involving Iran, prices have exceeded EUR 700 per tonne and reached up to EUR 800 per tonne in some Member States. At the same time, farmers face rising energy and fuel costs, as well as disruptions in supply chains, particularly in transport, logistics and packaging. These pressures further reduce already limited profit margins. In this context: 1.
What urgent measures is the Commission considering to stabilise fertiliser prices and address the impact of the CBAM on agriculture?
Does the Commission intend to mobilise financial support, including under the common agricultural policy or the crisis reserve, to offset rising energy and fuel costs?
What concrete actions will the Commission take to strengthen the resilience of EU agricultural supply chains and reduce external dependencies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission is closely monitoring fertiliser and energy markets through the EU Fertilisers Market Observatory1. Concerning fertilisers, measures already taken include the decision for temporary duty-free tariff rate quotas for ammonia, urea and several other key nitrogen fertilisers (except for imports from Russia and Belarus) for a period of one year until 31 May 2027, a reduced carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) default value markup of 1%, and the adoption of a State aid Framework on the Middle East2. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted a Fertiliser Action Plan3, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience. The Commission will deliver, ahead of the next production cycle, targeted exceptional support through the agricultural reserve to European farmers facing high fertiliser costs, and a legislative package proposal which will include a liquidity relief measure as a possibility under Member States’ Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans. To strengthen long term resilience, the Fertiliser Action Plan contains actions to increase EU fertiliser production capacity, support decarbonisation of the sector, diversify supply chains, improve market transparency, promote nutrient recycling, to reduce dependency on imported fossil fuels and other inputs. The Commission is also working on measures supporting strategic autonomy across the agri-food chain and the rest of the economy including energy and fertilisers.
